title: Project Overview
text:
Every retail dataset has its heroes and villains — vendors that drive growth, and others that quietly trap cash. I built a vendor performance model using SQL, Python, and statistical analysis to uncover who’s driving sales, who’s protecting margins, and where money gets stuck.
What started as raw transactions turned into a clear story of leverage, pricing behavior, and capital flow — revealing exactly where the business gains power, and where it leaks it.

Data Modeling

Raw Layer: Direct extracts from operational systems.
Staging Layer: Standardized formats, validated joins, and removed incomplete vendor records.
Mart Layer: Aggregated vendor and brand-level metrics into mart.vendor_sales_summary (~10K records).

Result: A unified, analysis-ready dataset combining sales, purchasing, inventory, and vendor-level information — enabling precise profitability and performance analysis.

title: Project Overview
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
The first step was to understand the structure and reliability of mart.vendor_sales_summary. I profiled each variable to check distributions, missing values, and potential outliers before moving to deeper analysis.

Key Observations

Scale: 10,692 records across 128 vendors and over 10,600 brands — most brands tied to a single vendor.
Price Extremes: Purchase and selling prices show upper outliers, likely premium or imported products.
Profitability: Mean profit_margin of -15.89 with high variance, reflecting loss-leading or inconsistent pricing.
Gross Profit Range: From -52K to 1.29M — a mix of profitable and loss-making transactions.
Efficiency Gap: sales_to_purchase_ratio varies widely (mean 2.55, max 352.9), revealing large performance disparities.
Inventory Turnover: Median stock_turnover around 0.98 indicates slow-moving inventory for most vendors.
Scale Variance: Wide spread in total sales and purchase dollars — large vendors dominate, smaller ones occupy niche spaces.



Data Quality

Slightly incomplete metrics (sales_quantity, gross_profit, profit_margin) point to limited missing data.
High standard deviations and skewed distributions suggest the need for transformation and outlier treatment in later stages.

Key Insights from Summary Statistics
Negative & Zero Values

Gross Profit: Minimum value of –52,002.78 indicates certain products were sold at a loss, possibly due to high costs or discount-driven sales.
Profit Margin: Approaches –∞ in some cases, suggesting transactions with zero or negative revenue.
Sales Quantity and Sales Dollars: Contain zeros, reflecting items purchased but never sold — likely slow-moving or obsolete stock.

High Variance and Outliers

Purchase and Actual Prices: Maximum values (5,681.81 and 7,499.99) far exceed the mean, reflecting premium or imported products.
Freight Cost: Ranges from 0.09 to 257,032.07, indicating large shipment discrepancies or inefficient logistics.
Stock Turnover: Spans from 0 to 274.5; ratios above 1 imply that previous stock fulfilled new sales, highlighting uneven inventory cycles.



Distribution of Numerical Variables
To understand how each metric behaves, I visualized the distributions for all numeric columns. My objective was simple, spot skewness, outliers, and patterns that hint at where value and inefficiency concentrate.
Observations:

Most variables are right-skewed, showing that a few vendors dominate while the rest cluster at lower values.
total_sales_dollars and gross_profit have heavy tails, confirming that a small group drives most of the revenue and profit.
profit_margin includes negative values, pointing to loss-making or heavily discounted transactions.
freight_cost and stock_turnover behave differently — their wider spread suggests operational variability worth investigating later.

In short, the data behaves like many real-world markets: a handful of players account for most of the movement, and the long tail holds the inefficiencies waiting to be optimized.

Outlier Detection

(Figure: Box plots showing distribution and outliers for all numerical variables.)



Data Filtering Criteria
To ensure analytical accuracy, I applied a set of logical filters to remove invalid or incomplete records. The focus was on retaining only transactions that reflected genuine sales and profitability.
Filtering Conditions:

gross_profit > 0 — retained only profitable transactions.
profit_margin > 0 — excluded loss-making or zero-margin entries.
total_sales_quantity > 0 — ensured only records with actual sales activity remained.

After applying these conditions, the dataset reduced from 10,692 to 8,564 records — eliminating roughly 20% of inconsistent or non-representative entries. This refined dataset now provides a cleaner foundation for modeling vendor performance and profitability.

Distribution After Cleaning
After filtering out invalid records, I re-examined the numerical distributions to confirm the impact of data cleaning. The updated histograms show noticeably reduced skewness and fewer extreme outliers, especially in profitability and pricing variables.
Key Observations:

Profit Margin: Now stabilizes between 25%–40%, representing a realistic range for healthy vendor profitability.
Gross Profit & Total Sales Price: Still right-skewed, as a few major vendors continue to drive most of the revenue — typical for retail ecosystems.
Freight Cost: Distribution tightened significantly, confirming that most anomalous shipping values were successfully filtered.
Stock Turnover & Sales-to-Purchase Ratio: Retain long tails, highlighting variability in vendor efficiency and inventory flow — a point for deeper analysis later.



Show code
plt.figure(figsize=(15,10))
for i, col in enumerate(numerical_cols):
    plt.subplot(4,4,i+1) #Adjust grid layout as needed
    sns.histplot(df[col],kde=True, bins=30)
    plt.title(col)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









(Figure: Distributions of numerical variables after cleaning, showing reduced skewness and improved data consistency.)
Conclusion: Post-cleaning, the dataset reflects valid and profit-generating vendor activity, ensuring that all subsequent analyses rest on consistent and reliable data. This forms a clean foundation for comparative performance analysis across vendors and brands.


Categorical Feature Analysis
I examined the key categorical variables — vendor names and product descriptions — to understand how sales records are distributed across suppliers and brands.

Top Vendors and Products
The plots below show the top 10 vendors and top 10 products based on record frequency.


Show code

plt.figure(figsize=(12,5))
for i, col in enumerate(categorical_cols):
    plt.subplot(1,2,i+1)
    sns.countplot(y=df[col], order =df[col].value_counts().index[:10]) #top 10 categories
    plt.title(f"count plot of {col}")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









(Figure: Top 10 vendors and products by frequency, showing market concentration among key players.)
Insights:

MARTIGNETTI COMPANIES appears most frequently, followed by M S Walker Inc and Ultra Beverage Company LLP, highlighting their central role in the dataset.
Prominent vendors such as Perfecta Wines, E & J Gallo Winery, and Diageo North America Inc also maintain substantial representation.
On the product side, Southern Comfort, Bacardi Superior Rum, and Jägermeister Liqueur lead the list.
Repeated listings like Southern Comfort and Southern Comfort 100 Proof indicate SKU-level granularity within product tracking.

Summary: The dataset remains concentrated among a few large vendors and high-volume brands. Future analyses should account for vendor size to avoid bias when comparing profitability or performance metrics.



Correlation Analysis
To understand how different numerical variables interact, I computed a correlation matrix and visualized it as a heatmap. This provides a quick view of which metrics move together and which operate independently.


Show code
#correlational heatmap
plt.figure(figsize=(12,8))
correlation_matrix=df[numerical_cols].corr()
sns.heatmap(correlation_matrix, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="coolwarm", linewidths=0.5)
plt.title("correlation heatmap")
plt.show()









(Figure: Correlation heatmap showing relationships among pricing, sales, and profitability variables.)


Insights from the Heatmap

Pricing Relationship: purchase_price and actual_price are almost perfectly correlated (r = 0.99), reinforcing the presence of a cost-plus pricing structure.
Sales and Procurement Link: A strong correlation between total_purchase_dollars and total_sales_dollars (r = 0.96) shows that higher procurement volumes consistently translate to higher sales.
Profit Scales with Sales: gross_profit aligns closely with sales measures (r ≈ 0.96), confirming that top-selling products are also the main profit drivers.
Tax Alignment: total_excise_tax strongly tracks total_sales_dollars (r = 0.98), indicating consistent tax application relative to sales.
Profit Margin Independence: Weak correlation between profit_margin and other financial variables suggests margin variability across products — likely due to differing pricing or discount strategies.
Inventory Efficiency: A moderate correlation between stock_turnover and profit_margin (r = 0.42) indicates that faster-moving inventory tends to be more profitable.
Vendor Neutrality: vendor_number shows negligible correlation with performance metrics, confirming that vendor IDs themselves don’t drive performance outcomes.

Summary: The heatmap reveals a tightly connected sales–profit–tax structure, but also highlights inconsistency in profit margins across products. These gaps point toward opportunities in pricing optimization and inventory efficiency tuning.

Analysis 1 — High-Margin, Low-Sales Brands
Business Objective: Find the hidden gems, brands that quietly make great margins but barely move off the shelf. These are the ones that don’t need a miracle, just a nudge.

Approach
I aggregated performance data at the brand level, combining total_sales_dollars and average profit_margin. From there, percentile thresholds (15th for low sales, 85th for high margin) defined an objective filter for underperforming but profitable brands.


Step 1 — Roll Up the Data
I grouped everything at the brand level, pulling together total_sales_dollars and average profit_margin. The idea was simple: who’s making the most money per sale, and who’s actually selling enough to matter?

Step 5 — Zoom In
Because big vendors can distort the picture, I zoomed in on brands making under $8,000 in total sales. The pattern held — the same cluster of high-margin brands sat neatly above the margin threshold line.

plt.axvline(low_sales_threshold, linestyle='--', color='black', label="Los sales Threshold")

plt.ylabel("profit margin (%)")

Findings
Here’s what the data actually says: * Profit-rich but volume-poor. These brands make excellent margins but remain underexposed. * The upper-left cluster of the scatter plot captures these outliers clearly, separating them from the broader dataset. * The profit margin range (≈65–90%) shows strong pricing power, while sales volumes remain limited — often due to low visibility or shelf turnover. * The majority of products sit below the high-margin line, confirming that broad profitability remains moderate. * The clean separation between the clusters suggests structural inefficiency rather than random variance — a consistent group of brands is systematically underselling.
Interpretation: These brands are not problem products — they’re quiet winners trapped by low exposure. With already strong margins, even a small lift in volume could drive a significant uptick in overall profit.

Business Takeaway
This isn’t a problem — it’s an opportunity hiding in plain sight. Brands with high margins and low sales are primed for bundling, cross-selling, or targeted campaigns. A small marketing push or strategic price adjustment could turn them from quiet performers into profit accelerators.

section: Analysis 2 — Top Vendors and Brands by Sales
text:
Analysis 2 — Top Vendors and Brands by Sales
Objective: Identify which vendors and brands drive the majority of total sales to pinpoint key revenue contributors.
I aggregated total_sales_dollars at both the vendor and brand levels to see who’s really moving the market. When ranked and visualized side by side, the pattern became obvious — a few heavyweights dominate both supply and consumer demand.

def format_dollars(value):
    if value >= 1_000_000:
        return f"{value/1_000_000:.2f}M"
    elif value >= 1_000:
        return f"{value/1_000:.2f}k"
    else:
        return str(value)


top_brands.apply(lambda x: format_dollars(x))

plt.figure(figsize=(15,5))

#plot for top vendors

plt.title("top 10 vendors by sales")

for bar in ax1.patches:
    ax1.text(bar.get_width()+ (bar.get_width()*0.02),
             bar.get_y()+ bar.get_height()/2,
             format_dollars(bar.get_width()),
             ha='left', va='center', fontsize=10, color='black')

# plot for top brands

plt.subplot(1,2,2)
ax2=sns.barplot(y=top_brands.index.astype(str), x=top_brands.values, palette="Reds_r")
plt.title("Top 10 brands by sales")

for bar in ax2.patches:
    ax2.text(bar.get_width()+ (bar.get_width()*0.02),
             bar.get_y()+bar.get_height()/2,
             format_dollars(bar.get_width()),
             ha='left', va='center', fontsize=10, color='black')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









(Figure: Comparative bar charts of top 10 vendors and brands by total sales, highlighting revenue concentration among leading players.)
At the brand level, the story mirrors the vendor hierarchy. Jack Daniels No 7 Black tops the list at $7.96M, closely followed by Tito’s Handmade Vodka and Grey Goose Vodka. Premium spirits dominate across the board — not because of discounts or volume plays, but because brand trust and consistency sell better than price ever could.
The data confirms a top-heavy market. A few established vendors and globally recognized brands command the lion’s share of sales, while smaller vendors occupy the long tail — important, but easily overshadowed. This imbalance signals where negotiation leverage lies and where emerging players need to invest in visibility, differentiation, or category focus to compete.
Takeaway: The sales distribution underscores a highly consolidated market led by major vendors and globally recognized brands. These insights can guide partnership prioritization, negotiation strategy, and promotional planning.

Negotiate smarter with top suppliers to capture volume-based cost advantages.
Diversify the vendor base to protect against supply disruption.
Continuously monitor high-volume vendors to ensure reliability and cost efficiency.

This kind of structure works well for bulk discounts but leaves the business exposed to supply disruption or pricing shifts from a handful of partners.

A balanced strategy would involve:

Negotiating multi-year terms or rebates with the top vendors to secure volume advantages.
Introducing secondary suppliers for high-value categories to reduce dependency.
Monitoring vendor performance regularly to ensure reliability and continuity.

In short, procurement efficiency is high — but resilience will depend on how well vendor concentration is managed moving forward.

Analysis 6 — Profit Margin Confidence Intervals: Top vs. Low Vendors
I wanted to see whether the most successful vendors actually make more money per sale — or if, like most high-volume businesses, they trade margin for scale. To check, I split vendors into two groups: top performers (top 25% by sales) and low performers (bottom 25%). Then I calculated their mean profit margins and 95% confidence intervals.


Show code
top_threshold= df['total_sales_dollars'].quantile(0.75)
low_threshold= df['total_sales_dollars'].quantile(0.25)

top_vendors = df[df["total_sales_dollars"] >= top_threshold]["profit_margin"].dropna()
low_vendors = df[df["total_sales_dollars"] <= low_threshold]["profit_margin"].dropna()
# to calculate the confidence interval
def confidence_interval(data, confidence=0.95):
    mean_val=np.mean(data)
    std_err=np.std(data,ddof=1)/np.sqrt(len(data)) #standard error
    t_critical=stats.t.ppf((1+confidence)/2, df=len(data)-1)
    margin_of_error= t_critical *std_err
    return mean_val, mean_val-margin_of_error, mean_val+margin_of_error
# Compute confidence intervals for top and low vendors
top_mean, top_lower, top_upper = confidence_interval(top_vendors)
low_mean, low_lower, low_upper = confidence_interval(low_vendors)

# Print results
print(f"Top Vendors 95% CI: ({top_lower:.2f}, {top_upper:.2f}), Mean: {top_mean:.2f}")
print(f"Low Vendors 95% CI: ({low_lower:.2f}, {low_upper:.2f}), Mean: {low_mean:.2f}")

# Plot comparison
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))

# --- Top Vendors Plot ---

plt.axvline(top_upper, color="blue", linestyle="--", label=f"Top Upper: {top_upper:.2f}")
plt.axvline(top_mean, color="blue", linestyle="-", label=f"Top Mean: {top_mean:.2f}")

Help low vendors scale up by improving distribution or exposure — they’ve already got strong unit profitability.

section: Analysis 7 — Hypothesis Testing: Profit Margin Differences Between Vendor Groups
text:
Analysis 7 — Hypothesis Testing: Profit Margin Differences Between Vendor Groups
I wanted to confirm whether the profit gap I observed between top vendors and low vendors was just noise — or if it actually held up statistically.

Hypotheses

H₀: No significant difference exists in average profit margins between top- and low-performing vendors.
H₁: There is a significant difference in mean profit margins between the two groups.



Method
I ran a two-sample t-test assuming unequal variances.

Top vendors: sales above the 75th percentile
Low vendors: sales below the 25th percentile

This test checks whether their mean profit margins come from the same population.


Show code
from scipy.stats import ttest_ind

# Define thresholds for top and low vendors (based on quartiles)
top_threshold = df["total_sales_dollars"].quantile(0.75)
low_threshold = df["total_sales_dollars"].quantile(0.25)

# Split vendors into top and low based on sales
top_vendors = df[df["total_sales_dollars"] >= top_threshold]["profit_margin"].dropna()
low_vendors = df[df["total_sales_dollars"] <= low_threshold]["profit_margin"].dropna()

# Perform Two-Sample T-Test
t_stat, p_value = ttest_ind(top_vendors, low_vendors, equal_var=False)

# Print results
print(f"T-Statistic: {t_stat:.4f}, P-Value: {p_value:.4f}")

if p_value < 0.05:
    print("Reject H₀: There is a significant difference in profit margins between top and low-performing vendors.")
else:
    print("Fail to Reject H₀: No significant difference in profit margins.")


T-Statistic: -17.6695, P-Value: 0.0000
Reject H₀: There is a significant difference in profit margins between top and low-performing vendors.




Results

(Figure: Output of two-sample t-test comparing profit margins between top and low vendors.)

The p-value rounds to zero — meaning the difference isn’t by chance. Low-performing vendors genuinely earn higher margins than the top ones.


What This Means
High-performing vendors run a volume game — low margins, big throughput, and tight pricing. Low-performing vendors sit on the other side — fewer sales but stronger markups, likely in premium or niche categories.
This confirms two distinct business models:

Top vendors: Win on efficiency and scale.
Low vendors: Win on exclusivity and price control.



Takeaway
The profit gap isn’t just visible — it’s statistically significant. The data backs a dual vendor strategy:

Push cost optimization and scale for top performers.
Expand reach for high-margin, low-volume vendors to capture untapped growth.
